newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS - DBS pays premium for healthcare.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - DBS pays premium for healthcare.

text.p: Property blue chip DBS Land Ltd is paying a huge premium for a stake in healthcare group Parkway Holdings Ltd but the move is seen as a strategic one in the long term, investment analysts said on Monday.

DBS Land said last week it had agreed to buy a 19.2 percent stake in Parkway for Singapore $391 million (US$273 million) or at S$6.50 a share, giving the healthcare group a 1997 price earnings multiple of about 34 times.

Analysts note the PE is double the Singapore market average of 17 times for 1997 and also sharply higher than the PE of about 21 times for the much smaller Raffles Medical Group when it went public in March.
"It is expensive for DBS Land. Basically, in the next 12 months, there will be no positive contribution from Parkway," Ng Yeow Tong, GK Goh investment analyst, said.
He said DBS land's return from Parkway works out to be about three percent while financing cost for the deal could be about four to five percent a year.
"At best it will be neutral if Parkway profits jump sharply. But at worst, it will be negative on the bottomline" he said.
Lim Chung Chun, analyst with ING Baring Securities, agreed. "The short-term impact on DBS Land's bottomline will be negative as they bought the shares at quite an expensive price," he said.
But over the longer term, the acquisition would mean DBS Land, in which government linked DBS Bank is a majority shareholder, would have another source of recurring income, Lim said.
DBS Land's income is currently from property development, rentals from several commercial buildings and also from its hotel operations. Last year, it made net profit of S$207 million.

Analysts said the regional healthcare business, in which Parkway is a major player owning several hospitals in Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia with some 1,700 beds, should see significant growth in the new few years.
Parkway's 1996 net profit had doubled to S$48 million and is expected to show annual growth of about 15 percent in the next couple of years.
Analysts said while prospects for private healthcare look good with rising affluence, competition was also heating up.
"If you look at Malaysia, many private hospitals and medical centres have come up in Kuala Lumpur, Malacca and Penang. And more are sprouting up," said an analyst with a Singapore bank.
She said the competition would continue to be keen and it was hard to justify the premium DBS Land was paying for Parkway.

DBS Land chief executive officer and deputy chairman Han Cheng Fong dismissed such concerns. "We don't think it is expensive. If we thought it was expensive, we won't have bought it," he said at a recent briefing.
Some analysts also speculate that DBS Land's government links could be an element in the move.

"It could be the government is worried about private healthcare costs in Singapore going out of control. So they want to have some control through a government linked company like DBS Land," said one analyst who declined to be identified.
